loop.meaning: Extremely cheap or miserly, often used to describe someone who goes to great lengths to save a tiny amount of money.
loop.example: Bro is so chindi, he asked for a refund on a 10-rupee chai.

loop.example: She keeps bringing her ex into our arguments just to make me insecure; that's classic triangulation.

loop.meaning: Non-Resident Indians; Indian citizens who live abroad for work, education, or permanent residence.
loop.example: Half the comments on that reel complaining about Indian traffic are from delusional NRIs.
loop.context: Ubiquitous in Indian internet culture, especially when discussing cultural disconnect or diaspora behavior.

loop.meaning: When an attempted solution to a problem accidentally makes the problem worse due to unintended perverse incentives.
loop.example: Giving a bounty for every stray rat just led people to start breeding rats for easy cash; absolute cobra effect.
loop.context: Referenced in economics and policy discussions when pointing out failed bureaucratic interventions.

loop.meaning: A classic Indian meme phenomenon where random live streams or videos of a JCB earthmover digging dirt attract millions of mesmerized viewers.

loop.meaning: Carefree, fearless, and living life on one's own terms without worrying about what others think.

passage.text: Her husband, among various physical accomplishments, had been one of the most powerful ends that ever played football at New Haven—a national figure in a way, one of those men who reach such an acute limited excellence at twenty-one that everything afterward savours of anticlimax. His family were enormously wealthy—even in college his freedom with money was a matter for reproach—but now he’d left Chicago and come East in a fashion that rather took your breath away: for instance, he’d brought down a string of polo ponies from Lake Forest. It was hard to realize that a man in my own generation was wealthy enough to do that.
passage.author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
passage.context: Describing Tom Buchanan, a college football star whose peak arrived at age twenty-one.

ideas.title: Your brain uses two different thinking systems
ideas.text: Your mind relies on a fast, automatic system for quick guesses and a slow, logical system for tough problems. The fast system jumps to conclusions when you see a stranger's angry face before knowing the context. Pause for five seconds before reacting to a heated message today.

ideas.title: First impressions heavily distort later judgments
ideas.text: The halo effect makes you assume someone good at one thing is brilliant at everything else. If a professor wears a sharp suit, you might wrongly think their lecture is flawless. Notice if your opinion of a new acquaintance is based on just one trait today.

ideas.title: Losses hurt much more than gains feel good
ideas.text: Loss aversion means the pain of dropping fifty rupees hits harder than the joy of finding it. Investors panic and sell stocks at a bottom just to stop the bleeding. Identify one minor fear of missing out that is currently driving your choices today.

ideas.title: We rely too much on easily remembered stories
ideas.text: The availability heuristic tricks us into thinking dramatic events happen constantly because we recall them vividly. After seeing news about a plane crash, you might irrationally fear flying more than driving. Check if your current worry is based on a viral news story today.

ideas.title: Past random successes create false confidence
ideas.text: Survivorship bias makes us copy the habits of extreme outliers while ignoring thousands who failed with the same strategy. Dropping out of college worked for Steve Jobs, but it ruined many others. Question whether your career idol succeeded through skill or sheer luck today.

ideas.title: We ignore baseline statistics for vivid tales
ideas.text: The narrative fallacy makes us prefer a compelling personal story over boring statistical averages. You might buy a notoriously unreliable phone because your cousin had a good experience with it. Look up the actual failure rates of a gadget or course before buying it today.

ideas.title: Focusing too narrowly blinds you to reality
ideas.text: What you see is all there is, meaning your brain builds a complete story from very limited evidence. When preparing for an exam, you often forget to factor in unexpected fatigue or sick days. Write down three missing variables in your current big life plan today.
